title: Where do Alice and Bob land?
hook: Eve overhears every number Alice and Bob send. Follow their moves round a 23-hour clock.

knows: how a clock wraps from the last hour back to the first
doesNotKnow: that two people can agree on a secret number while someone hears everything they send

misconception: Two strangers cannot agree on a secret over a channel an eavesdropper hears completely.
objective: The learner can explain why Bob (8 multiplied 15 times) and Alice (19 multiplied 6 times) land on the same mark of the 23-clock: both are 5 multiplied 90 times, while Eve heard only 8 and 19.

claims.text: On a 23-hour clock, starting at 1 and multiplying by 5 six times stops on 8; multiplying by 5 fifteen times stops on 19.
claims.source: 5^6 mod 23 = 8 and 5^15 mod 23 = 19. Demo.tsx walk(5, 6) and walk(5, 15); builder re-ran in Node with BigInt: 8n, 19n. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node BigInt: 5^6 = 8, 5^15 = 19 (mod 23).

claims.text: From 1, multiplying by 8 fifteen times and multiplying by 19 six times both stop on 2.
claims.source: 8^15 mod 23 = 2 = 19^6 mod 23. Demo.tsx BOB[15] and ALICE[6]; builder re-ran in Node: 2 and 2. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 8^15 = 2, 19^6 = 2 (mod 23).

claims.text: Multiplying by 5 ninety times (6 × 15) from 1 on the 23-clock also stops on 2, because each side multiplied 5 by itself 90 times.
claims.source: (5^6)^15 = (5^15)^6 = 5^90; 5^90 mod 23 = 2 (Demo.tsx DIRECT; Node check). Wrapping after each multiply gives the same result as wrapping at the end (arithmetic modulo n). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 5^90 mod 23 = 2.

claims.text: Multiply, then wrap around the clock, is the same as keeping the remainder after dividing by 23.
claims.source: Definition of multiplication modulo n (e.g. Hardy and Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, ch. 5, congruences). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

claims.text: Eve hears only 8 and 19, never the secrets 6 or 15, yet on a 23-clock she could find a secret by trying every one.
claims.source: Exhaustive search over exponents 1..22 in Node: 5^6 = 8 and 5^15 = 19 are found in 22 tries. The public messages in the protocol are only the clock, base and the two public numbers (Diffie and Hellman 1976). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: exhaustive search finds 8 at exponent 6 and 19 at exponent 15, within 22 tries.

claims.text: Real systems use enormous clocks where trying every secret is hopeless.
claims.source: Diffie-Hellman security rests on the discrete-logarithm problem being infeasible for large moduli (Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography', IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 22(6), 1976). No key size is stated in the lesson. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Large-modulus hardness is the standard Diffie-Hellman security assumption; no key size claimed.

claims.text: This scheme is the Diffie-Hellman key exchange.
claims.source: Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 22(6), 1976. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Diffie and Hellman 1976, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 22(6):644-654, correct.

recall.question: Alice and Bob each keep a secret number and send only a public result. Why do they end up with the same shared number?
options: Both have multiplied the base by itself (secret A × secret B) times
They both send their secrets, but scrambled
recall.why: Each multiplies the other's public number by their own secret count, so both reach the base multiplied (A × B) times; the secrets never travel.
